size: Adults commonly 1–1.5 m; larger individuals are recorded.

images.alt: An Indian cobra raising its body with its hood spread, showing a dark spectacle-like marking, among low green leaves.
images.creator: Unknown (stock photograph)
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief

en.summary: A widespread elapid of the lowlands, famous for the hood it spreads when it feels threatened, and deeply woven into Sri Lankan culture.
en.appearance: A medium-sized snake with smooth, glossy scales. When disturbed it raises the front part of its body and spreads its neck ribs into a hood. Many individuals show a pale, spectacle-like mark on the back of the hood.
en.variation: Colour ranges from pale yellowish brown to dark brown or almost black. The hood marking can be bold, faint or broken, and juveniles may look noticeably different from adults.
en.ecology: Feeds mainly on rodents, frogs and toads. Often shelters in termite mounds, rodent burrows and gaps in walls, which brings it close to farms and villages.
en.behaviour: Active mostly around dusk and at night, though it is also seen by day. It usually retreats when given space.
en.defence: Raises its head, spreads the hood and hisses. It may make bluff strikes before biting if it is cornered or handled.
en.distribution: Recorded across much of the island's lowlands in both the wet and dry zones.
en.limitations: A cobra does not always display its hood, and other snakes, such as rat snakes and keelbacks, can raise their heads or flatten their necks. Never use the presence or absence of a hood to decide whether a snake is dangerous.
en.folklore: The naga (cobra) holds a respected place in Sri Lankan Buddhist and Hindu traditions. A widely told Buddhist story describes Mucalinda, a naga king, sheltering the meditating Buddha from a storm with his hood. Many families avoid harming cobras for these reasons.

si.summary: පහත්බිම් පුරා පැතිරී සිටින, තර්ජනයක් දැනුණු විට පෙණය විහිදුවන, ශ්‍රී ලාංකීය සංස්කෘතියට සමීපව බැඳුණු සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: தாழ்நிலங்களில் பரவலாகக் காணப்படும் இப்பாம்பு, அச்சுறுத்தப்படும்போது படம் விரிப்பதற்குப் பெயர் பெற்றது; இலங்கைப் பண்பாட்டுடன் நெருங்கிய தொடர்புடையது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

size: A heavy-bodied snake; adults commonly around 1 m.

en.summary: A stout viper of grasslands and paddy fields, and one of the snakes behind a large share of serious snakebites in Sri Lanka.
en.appearance: Thick-bodied with a broad, flattened, triangular head clearly wider than the neck. The back is usually light brown with three rows of dark oval blotches, each edged with black and a thin pale outline. The scales are strongly keeled, giving a rough, matt look.
en.variation: Background colour varies from greyish to reddish or yellowish brown, and the blotches can merge into chain-like rows.
en.ecology: Feeds largely on rodents, which draws it into paddy fields and farmland, especially around harvest time.
en.behaviour: Mainly active at night, resting in grass, crop stubble or under debris by day.
en.defence: Forms tight coils and produces a loud, sustained hiss. Strikes quickly if touched or stepped on.
en.distribution: Most frequently recorded in the dry and intermediate zone lowlands, with records from other parts of the island.
en.limitations: Young pythons and some harmless snakes also carry blotched patterns. Mud, shedding and poor light can hide the markings completely.

si.summary: තණබිම් සහ කුඹුරුවල වෙසෙන, ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ බරපතළ සර්ප දෂ්ට කිරීම් විශාල ප්‍රමාණයකට හේතු වන ඝන සිරුරැති පොළඟෙකි.

ta.summary: புல்வெளிகளிலும் வயல்களிலும் வாழும் தடித்த உடலுடைய விரியன்; இலங்கையில் கடுமையான பாம்புக்கடிகளில் பெரும் பங்கிற்குக் காரணமானது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A glossy, night-active elapid of villages and farmland. Its bite can be almost painless, which is why prevention matters so much.
en.appearance: Shiny black or bluish black with thin, paired white crossbands that are usually clearer towards the tail. A row of enlarged, hexagonal scales runs along the middle of the back.
en.variation: Bands may be faint or incomplete, particularly on the front of the body.
en.ecology: Feeds largely on other snakes, as well as lizards, frogs and small rodents.
en.behaviour: Strictly nocturnal. By day it hides in burrows, leaf piles or gaps in buildings and tends to tuck its head under its coils.
en.defence: Usually reluctant to bite when disturbed by day. Bites often happen at night to people sleeping on the floor.
en.distribution: Most often recorded in the dry zone lowlands, including around homes.
en.limitations: Harmless wolf snakes have similar banded patterns and are frequently confused with kraits, in both directions.

si.summary: ගම්මාන සහ ගොවිබිම්වල රාත්‍රියේ ක්‍රියාශීලී වන දිලිසෙන සර්පයෙකි. එහි දෂ්ට කිරීම බොහෝ විට වේදනා රහිත විය හැකි බැවින් වැළැක්වීම ඉතා වැදගත් ය.

ta.summary: கிராமங்களிலும் வேளாண் நிலங்களிலும் இரவில் சுறுசுறுப்பாக இருக்கும் பளபளப்பான பாம்பு. இதன் கடி வலியற்றதாக இருக்கலாம்; எனவே தடுப்பு மிக முக்கியம்.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A krait found only in Sri Lanka, living in the wet zone's forests, plantations and gardens.
en.appearance: Black with white or greyish crossbands. In many individuals the bands are broad and ring-like, especially in juveniles.
en.variation: Bands can fade with age, and some adults appear mostly dark.
en.ecology: Like other kraits, it is thought to feed mainly on other snakes and small vertebrates.
en.behaviour: Nocturnal and secretive, sheltering under logs, rocks and leaf litter by day.
en.defence: Generally shy; bites are associated with accidental contact, often at night.
en.distribution: Recorded from the wet zone and adjoining hills.
en.limitations: Easily confused with the common krait and with harmless wolf snakes.

si.summary: තෙත් කලාපයේ වනාන්තර, වතු සහ ගෙවතුවල වෙසෙන, ශ්‍රී ලංකාවට පමණක් ආවේණික කරවලෙකි.

ta.summary: ஈர வலயக் காடுகள், தோட்டங்கள், வீட்டுத் தோட்டங்களில் வாழும், இலங்கைக்கு மட்டுமே உரிய கட்டு விரியன் இனம்.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

size: Small; adults usually well under 1 m.

en.summary: A small viper of sandy, dry coastal scrub, known for the rasping warning sound made by its own scales.
en.appearance: A small, rough-scaled viper with a pear-shaped head. Usually sandy or brownish with pale, wavy or zigzag markings along the sides and darker blotches on the back.
en.variation: Colour tends to match local soil and sand.
en.ecology: Feeds on small vertebrates and invertebrates, including scorpions, frogs and lizards.
en.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; often hides partly buried in sand or under low vegetation.
en.defence: Forms C-shaped coils and rubs its saw-edged side scales together, producing a rasping sound. Strikes quickly if pressed.
en.distribution: Restricted to dry coastal areas of the north and north-west of the island.
en.limitations: Its small size and camouflage make it easy to miss or to confuse with other small brown snakes.

si.summary: වැලි සහිත වියළි වෙරළබඩ පඳුරු බිම්වල වෙසෙන, තම කොරපොතු ඇතිල්ලීමෙන් අනතුරු ඇඟවීමේ ශබ්දයක් නගන කුඩා පොළඟෙකි.

ta.summary: மணற்பாங்கான வறண்ட கடலோரப் புதர்களில் வாழும் சிறிய விரியன்; தன் செதில்களை உரசி எச்சரிக்கை ஒலி எழுப்புவதற்குப் பெயர் பெற்றது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

images.alt: A coiled, reddish-brown hump-nosed viper with dark blotches and an upturned snout resting on a mossy log.
images.creator: Unknown
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief (BEEZ blog)

en.summary: A small, superbly camouflaged pit viper of leaf litter and home gardens, and a frequent cause of bites in the wet zone.
en.appearance: A small pit viper with a triangular head and a distinctive upturned snout. Brown, grey or reddish with darker blotches that blend into leaf litter.
en.variation: Colour and pattern vary considerably, even within one area.
en.ecology: Ambushes frogs, lizards and small mammals from leaf litter.
en.behaviour: Relies on staying still and camouflaged, so it is easily stepped on or touched while gardening or working on plantations.
en.defence: Bites quickly when touched or stepped on.
en.distribution: Recorded widely in the wet and intermediate zones, including gardens and plantations.
en.limitations: Sri Lanka has three hump-nosed vipers, H. hypnale and the endemic H. nepa and H. zara, which are very difficult to tell apart from photographs. The photograph shown is labelled to genus level only.

si.summary: කොළ රොඩු සහ ගෙවතුවල හොඳින් සැඟවී සිටින කුඩා පොළඟෙකි. තෙත් කලාපයේ දෂ්ට කිරීම්වලට නිතර හේතු වේ.

ta.summary: இலைக் குப்பைகளிலும் வீட்டுத் தோட்டங்களிலும் சிறப்பாக மறைந்து வாழும் சிறிய குழி விரியன்; ஈர வலயத்தில் அடிக்கடி கடிகளுக்குக் காரணமாகிறது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

images.alt: A bright green pit viper with bold black markings coiled around a dark branch, tongue extended.
images.creator: Damith Danthanarayana (as captioned in source)
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief

images.alt: A green pit viper stretched along a thin branch, its black-edged pattern visible.
images.creator: Unknown
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief

en.summary: A striking green viper found nowhere else on Earth, waiting motionless on branches in the island's forests and plantations.
en.appearance: Bright to yellowish green with black markings that often form a wavy line along the back. It has a triangular head, a heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril, and a prehensile tail for gripping branches.
en.variation: The amount of black varies widely; some individuals are almost plain green.
en.ecology: An ambush predator of frogs, lizards, birds and small mammals.
en.behaviour: Arboreal and mostly active at night, often resting in the same spot for long periods.
en.defence: Gapes and strikes if touched. Bites usually happen when people reach into vegetation without looking.
en.distribution: Recorded mainly in the wet and intermediate zones, with some records from forests elsewhere.
en.limitations: Many harmless snakes are green too. Colour alone tells you nothing about whether a snake is venomous.

si.summary: ලෝකයේ වෙනත් කිසිම තැනක නොමැති, ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වනාන්තර හා වතුවල අතුමත නොසෙල්වී රැඳී සිටින දීප්තිමත් කොළ පැහැති පොළඟෙකි.

ta.summary: உலகில் வேறெங்கும் காணப்படாத, இலங்கையின் காடுகளிலும் தோட்டங்களிலும் கிளைகளில் அசையாமல் காத்திருக்கும் பச்சை விரியன்.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

size: Very slender; adults commonly 1–1.5 m long.

images.alt: A green vine snake among leaves in Sinharaja rainforest, its long pointed snout and keyhole-shaped pupil visible.
images.creator: Unknown (stock photograph)
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief

images.alt: Close-up of a vine snake's narrow, pointed green head with a horizontal pupil.
images.creator: Unknown
images.source: Image reference supplied in the project brief

en.summary: An impossibly slender tree snake with a pointed snout and keyhole-shaped pupils. Its genus name comes from Sinhala.
en.appearance: Extremely thin and long, with a sharply pointed snout and horizontal, keyhole-shaped pupils that give it good forward-facing vision. Usually bright green, with a pale line along each side of the belly.
en.variation: Some individuals are yellowish, brownish or greyish rather than green.
en.ecology: Hunts lizards and frogs by day, often waiting motionless before striking.
en.behaviour: Arboreal and diurnal. It moves through shrubs and trees by stretching across gaps between branches.
en.defence: Opens its mouth wide and inflates its body, revealing black-and-white skin between the scales. It may sway like a vine in the breeze.
en.distribution: Widely recorded in gardens and forests across the island. A 2020 taxonomic revision restricted Ahaetulla nasuta in the strict sense to Sri Lanka.
en.limitations: Several other slender green or brown snakes, including other Ahaetulla species and bronzebacks, can look similar.
en.folklore: The scientific genus name Ahaetulla comes from the Sinhala ඇහැටුල්ලා, often explained as "eye-plucker", reflecting a long-held belief that the snake strikes at people's eyes. There is no evidence that it targets eyes; its pointed head and habit of resting at face height in shrubs probably helped the belief spread.

si.summary: තියුණු හොම්බක් සහ යතුරු සිදුරක හැඩැති ඇස් ඇති ඉතා සිහින් ගස් සර්පයෙකි. එහි විද්‍යාත්මක ගණ නාමය සිංහලෙන් පැමිණ ඇත.

ta.summary: கூர்மையான மூக்கும் சாவித்துளை வடிவக் கண்மணிகளும் கொண்ட மிக மெல்லிய மரப்பாம்பு; இதன் அறிவியல் பேரினப் பெயர் சிங்களத்திலிருந்து வந்தது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

size: Long and fast; adults commonly 1.5–2 m.

en.summary: A long, fast, harmless snake that keeps rodent numbers in check around farms and homes.
en.appearance: Large, slender-bodied and quick, with big eyes. Olive to brown, often with dark crossbars towards the rear of the body and tail.
en.variation: Colour ranges from pale yellowish brown to dark olive.
en.ecology: Feeds mainly on rodents, and also frogs and birds, which makes it valuable around farms.
en.behaviour: Active by day, moving fast across open ground and climbing well.
en.defence: Inflates its throat, makes a growling hiss and may strike. Not venomous, but bites can still be painful.
en.distribution: Widespread across the island, including towns and farmland.
en.limitations: When it raises its head and inflates its throat, it is sometimes mistaken for a cobra.
en.folklore: A widespread belief in Sri Lanka and India holds that rat snakes are male cobras, or that the two mate. They are different species in different families and do not interbreed.

si.summary: ගොවිබිම් සහ නිවෙස් අවට මීයන් පාලනය කරන, දිගු, වේගවත්, විෂ නැති සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: பண்ணைகளிலும் வீடுகளைச் சுற்றியும் எலிகளைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தும் நீண்ட, வேகமான, நஞ்சற்ற பாம்பு.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

size: The island's largest snake; large adults exceed 3 m.

en.summary: Sri Lanka's largest snake, a non-venomous constrictor of the dry zone's forests and wetlands.
en.appearance: Heavy and muscular, pale tan to greyish with large, dark-edged brown blotches along the back and an arrowhead-shaped mark on top of the head.
en.variation: Background colour and blotch shape vary between individuals.
en.ecology: Constricts mammals, birds and reptiles. Large individuals can take surprisingly large prey.
en.behaviour: Slow-moving on land, often travelling in a straight line; also swims well. Mostly active at night.
en.defence: Hisses and may bite if handled. Not venomous, but large pythons can cause serious bite wounds.
en.distribution: Recorded mainly in the dry zone lowlands, often near water.
en.limitations: Young pythons are sometimes confused with Russell's vipers because of their blotched pattern.
en.folklore: A common belief claims pythons hypnotise prey with their stare. There is no evidence for this; like other snakes, pythons have no eyelids and so seem to stare constantly.

si.summary: වියළි කලාපයේ වනාන්තර සහ තෙත්බිම්වල වෙසෙන, ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ විශාලතම සර්පයා වන විෂ නැති වෙළෙන සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: வறண்ட வலயக் காடுகளிலும் ஈரநிலங்களிலும் வாழும், இலங்கையின் மிகப்பெரிய பாம்பு; நஞ்சற்ற, இரையைச் சுற்றி நெரிக்கும் பாம்பு.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A common water snake of ponds, canals and paddy fields, patterned like a chessboard.
en.appearance: Olive, yellowish or brown with dark spots arranged in a checkerboard pattern. The scales are keeled.
en.variation: The checkered pattern can be sharp, faded or partly striped.
en.ecology: Feeds mainly on fish and frogs.
en.behaviour: Semi-aquatic, often seen swimming or resting at the water's edge, by day or night.
en.defence: Flattens its neck, raises its head and bites readily if handled. It is not venomous.
en.distribution: Widespread wherever there is fresh water.
en.limitations: Its neck-flattening display is sometimes mistaken for a cobra's hood.

si.summary: පොකුණු, ඇළ මාර්ග සහ කුඹුරුවල බහුලව දක්නට ලැබෙන, චෙස් පුවරුවක් වැනි රටාවක් ඇති ජල සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: குளங்கள், கால்வாய்கள், வயல்களில் பொதுவாகக் காணப்படும், சதுரங்கப் பலகை போன்ற வடிவமுடைய நீர்ப்பாம்பு.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A quick, slender tree snake with a bronze-brown back, often seen darting through garden shrubs.
en.appearance: Slender with large eyes and a bronze or brown back, paler flanks and belly.
en.variation: Several bronzeback species occur in Sri Lanka, some of them endemic, and they can look very similar.
en.ecology: Hunts lizards and frogs in trees and shrubs.
en.behaviour: Active by day, fast and agile in branches.
en.defence: Usually flees. May inflate its body to show bright skin between scales.
en.limitations: Identifying bronzebacks to species usually requires close examination of scales, which is not possible from a typical photograph.

si.summary: ගෙවතු පඳුරු අතරින් වේගයෙන් ගමන් කරන, ලෝකඩ-දුඹුරු පිටක් ඇති සිහින් ගස් සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: தோட்டப் புதர்களில் வேகமாக நகரும், வெண்கல-பழுப்பு முதுகுடைய மெல்லிய மரப்பாம்பு.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A harmless house snake whose banded pattern resembles a krait's, which shows why pattern alone can't be trusted.
en.appearance: Small and flattened-headed, brown with pale crossbands. The front teeth are enlarged, which gives the group its "wolf" name.
en.variation: Banding and colour vary; some individuals are faint or greyish.
en.ecology: Feeds mainly on geckos and skinks, often hunting on walls.
en.behaviour: Nocturnal; climbs walls and is common in and around houses.
en.defence: Bites readily if handled, but is not venomous.
en.limitations: Wolf snakes and kraits are routinely mistaken for each other. Treat any banded snake with caution and keep your distance.

si.summary: කරවලෙකුට සමාන ඉරි රටාවක් ඇති, විෂ නැති ගෘහාශ්‍රිත සර්පයෙකි. රටාව පමණක් විශ්වාස කළ නොහැකි බව එයින් පෙන්වයි.

ta.summary: கட்டு விரியனைப் போன்ற பட்டை வடிவமுடைய நஞ்சற்ற வீட்டுப் பாம்பு; வடிவத்தை மட்டும் நம்ப முடியாது என்பதை இது காட்டுகிறது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A tiny, worm-like burrowing snake that is often mistaken for an earthworm, and an all-female species.
en.appearance: Shiny dark brown to black, cylindrical, with a blunt head and tail and tiny, almost hidden eyes.
en.variation: Little variation; juveniles are simply smaller.
en.ecology: Feeds on ant and termite larvae and eggs underground.
en.behaviour: Lives in soil and leaf litter and surfaces after rain.
en.defence: Harmless. May press its tail tip against a hand when picked up.
en.distribution: Widespread in gardens and farmland. It has spread around the world in potted plants, earning the name "flowerpot snake".
en.limitations: Easily mistaken for an earthworm or for other blind snakes.
en.fact: Every known individual is female. The species reproduces by parthenogenesis, without males.

si.summary: පණුවෙකු ලෙස බොහෝ විට වරදවා වටහා ගන්නා, පසෙහි වෙසෙන ඉතා කුඩා සර්පයෙකි. මෙම විශේෂයේ සියල්ලම ගැහැනු සතුන් ය.

ta.summary: மண்புழு எனத் தவறாகக் கருதப்படும், மண்ணில் வாழும் மிகச் சிறிய பாம்பு; இவ்வினத்தில் அனைத்தும் பெண்களே.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.

en.summary: A marine elapid of shallow coasts and estuaries, most often met by fishers handling nets.
en.appearance: Grey to bluish grey with darker crossbands that fade in adults, a pointed snout and a flattened, paddle-shaped tail.
en.variation: Banding is usually clearer in juveniles.
en.ecology: Feeds mainly on fish in shallow coastal waters and estuaries.
en.behaviour: Fully aquatic and helpless on land.
en.defence: Bites when caught in nets or handled.
en.distribution: Recorded in coastal waters around the island.
en.limitations: Sea snakes, eels and some fish can be confused at a glance. Treat any snake-like animal in a net with care.

si.summary: නොගැඹුරු වෙරළ සහ කලපුවල වෙසෙන, දැල් හසුරුවන ධීවරයින්ට බොහෝ විට හමුවන මුහුදු සර්පයෙකි.

ta.summary: ஆழமற்ற கடற்கரைகளிலும் கழிமுகங்களிலும் வாழும் கடல் பாம்பு; வலைகளைக் கையாளும் மீனவர்கள் அடிக்கடி சந்திப்பது.

conservation.note: Assessment not yet recorded in this dataset.
